title: Selective conversion of methane to methanol at useful conversion under mild conditions

concept.text: The innovation is a continuous process that converts methane directly into methanol using molecular oxygen or air, while combining high methane conversion, high methanol selectivity and practically useful productivity under mild operating conditions. Conversion measures how much methane reacts; selectivity measures how much of the reacted carbon becomes methanol rather than other products. Success requires both together: selectively converting only a small fraction of the feed can leave a costly separation and recycle problem.

The intended capability is direct methane-to-methanol chemistry without first making synthesis gas. The oxidant requirement is part of the concept: a continuous room-temperature electrochemical process using carbonate as its oxygen source is relevant progress, but does not demonstrate the specified oxygen- or air-fed process. The supplied July 2025 study provides an example of that distinction.

significance.text: A successful direct process would change the production route to an existing commodity chemical, rather than create a previously unavailable substance. The supplied supplementary process analysis uses conventional syngas-based methanol production as its baseline. Bypassing that intermediate could simplify the route from methane to a transportable liquid, provided that the direct process's own reaction, separation and utility requirements preserve the advantage.

Conditional application: a compact, durable process could make some stranded or otherwise flared methane more practical to collect and convert into methanol. That outcome would also require suitable feed handling, product recovery, safe operation and favorable economics at the relevant scale. A selective catalyst alone would not demonstrate a deployable modular plant, and successful use at small sites would not establish competitiveness with large conventional methanol facilities.

The available carbonate-electrochemical process model illustrates why these qualifications matter: it includes gas and liquid recycle, separations, electricity demand and capital-cost assumptions. Its authors also acknowledge limited commercial cost data for gas-diffusion-electrode reactors and use water-electrolyzer cost data in their estimates. This analysis helps identify process burdens, but it neither establishes the economics of the proposed aerobic route nor supports a conclusion that it would displace conventional methanol production.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is sustained, selective partial oxidation with methane and O2 or air, at a combination of conversion, productivity, temperature and process burden that is useful beyond a laboratory demonstration. The supplied Nature Catalysis abstract identifies high selectivity in methane partial oxidation as challenging. Its carbonate-fed result does not establish this aerobic capability, while the supplied evidence is insufficient to establish that no other route had achieved it by November 1, 2026.

The research frames the chemical difficulty as activating methane's strong C–H bond while preventing further oxidation of the methanol product. This is a useful account of the proposed selectivity barrier, but the source intended to substantiate that explanation was not captured in the supplied review. It should therefore be retained as the research's mechanistic framing, rather than strengthened into a verified categorical claim that increasing conversion necessarily destroys methanol in every catalytic system.

Engineering synthesis: the breakthrough must extend from catalyst behavior to the whole process. Product must leave the reaction environment and be recovered without excessive dilution, recycle or energy use; catalyst activity and selectivity must persist; and the oxidant supply and operating conditions must remain practical. The supplied carbonate-process supplement documents recycle and subsequent separation requirements, supporting the need to evaluate integrated operation rather than a mass-normalized production rate alone.

The original research also contrasted the target with stepwise zeolite cycles, N2O-based oxidation and oleum-based platinum chemistry. Those comparisons identify potentially relevant neighboring approaches, but their performance and limitations were not substantiated by the supplied source texts. They cannot establish that every such approach leaves the same practical gap, nor can they substitute for evidence about continuous O2- or air-fed operation.

current_state.text: Kim and colleagues reported room-temperature electrochemical methane-to-methanol conversion in Nature Catalysis on July 4, 2025. The supplied review identifies IrO2 as the catalyst and carbonate as the oxygen source. The abstract reports a maximum methanol production rate of approximately 11.1 mmol gcat−1 h−1 under continuous operation. This is a documented advance in a related route, with an oxygen source different from the O2 or air specified for this innovation.

According to the supplied review, Supplementary Table 3 lists a flow-cell rate of 11,060 μmol gcat−1 h−1, equivalent to 11.06 mmol gcat−1 h−1, with 93% methanol selectivity at 25 °C and 1 bar. The table's 500 °C designation concerns catalyst preparation, not reaction temperature. The general selectivity challenge stated in the abstract should therefore not obscure the specific high selectivity reported for this experiment. Conversely, these figures alone do not establish high single-pass methane conversion, long-term durability or practical plant performance.

The evidence available to the supplied reviewer consisted of an abstract-level article preview and a separately retained, complete supplementary-information document. The full main article was not available in that material. Describing access as abstract-only would omit the supplement, while describing the complete main study as inspected would overstate access. The supplement's process and economic analyses are modeled evaluations, not demonstrations of commercial operation or modular stranded-gas deployment.

The original research cites a Molecular Catalysis prospect dated January 15, 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.mcat.2024.114721, as discussing the difficulty of mild selective methane oxidation and methanol overoxidation. No source artifact for that citation was supplied to the reviewer. Its characterization of the field and the wording attributed to it consequently remain unverified here; this access limitation is not evidence that the publication or its account is false.

The research also attributes to a JACS report dated April 10, 2024, DOI 10.1021/jacs.4c00646, transition-metal-free ferrierite oxidation with N2O at about 350 °C, a methanol production rate of 305 μmol g−1 min−1 and 89% methanol selectivity. These conditions and numerical results were not verified because no article artifact was supplied to the reviewer; the authors were also not expanded in the original extract. If confirmed, the reported result would concern an N2O route at elevated temperature, rather than establish the proposed mild aerobic process.

The supplied record contains no bounded search evidence establishing developments after the documented July 2025 result. It therefore supports a dated account of that advance, but not a definitive assessment of whether the proposed O2/air capability remained unmet on November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate continuously with methane and molecular oxygen or air, and report conversion, methanol selectivity, productivity and operating conditions together. Methanol should be the major carbon product, with single-pass conversion sufficient that separation and recycle do not erase the intended advantage over syngas-based production. This is a proposed evaluation framework, not an established industry or scientific standard; no fixed numerical temperature or selectivity threshold is adopted.
completion_criteria.label: Continuous operation demonstrates useful single-pass conversion with methanol predominance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: provide a closed carbon balance, an account of oxygen and other reagent inputs, identified byproducts, recovered methanol concentration and purity, and sustained operating data that reveal catalyst deactivation or regeneration requirements. Independent reproduction should test the central conversion–selectivity result under stated feed and reactor conditions. Tests across specified feed compositions and operating ranges would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, rather than universal performance.
completion_criteria.label: Closed process accounting and independently reproduced conversion–selectivity performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: publish an integrated material and energy balance and a transparent economic assessment for a modular stranded-gas application, including feed conditioning, oxygen or air supply, separation, recycle, catalyst replacement and capital costs. Compare it with an appropriate conventional alternative at the same scale and product specification. A modeled advantage should be identified as a projection until supported by relevant operating evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated stranded-gas economics compared against a matched conventional alternative

completion_criteria.text: A laboratory production rate in the millimole-per-gram-of-catalyst-per-hour range would not establish completion by itself. Its adequacy depends on conversion, product concentration, catalyst inventory, durability, energy use and the integrated plant balance. The supplied supplement's treatment of recycle and separation supports examining those burdens, but does not supply a universal minimum acceptable rate. The earlier numerical aspiration of more than 90% selectivity below 100 °C is not adopted as a completion standard, and its historical attribution remains unverified.
completion_criteria.label: Production rate adequacy assessed against integrated plant requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CHEMREV-06, mild nitrogen fixation competitive with Haber–Bosch, shares the ambition of replacing an established commodity-production route through difficult feedstock activation under milder conditions. Its chemistry and selectivity problem concern nitrogen fixation, whereas CHEMREV-12 concerns methane oxidation and methanol production. CHEMREV-11, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond in a complex molecule, overlaps in C–H activation, but adds positional choice and generality across complex substrates. CHEMREV-12 instead seeks one transformation at practical throughput. These are distinctions inferred from the supplied titles; the entries remain separate.

Roster-based comparison: CHEMREV-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request for arbitrary reactions, could encompass the ability to design a methane-oxidation catalyst, but requires a general catalyst-design capability far beyond success on this reaction. CHEMREV-01, prediction of realistic chemical outcomes before experiment, could help guide catalyst and process development without itself delivering methane conversion. CHEMREV-04, on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules, concerns much broader product access; this concept is focused on useful production of methanol from a specified feedstock.

Roster-based comparison: CHEMREV-07, fossil-competitive multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water, also couples chemical selectivity to process economics, but differs in carbon source and target products. Methane-to-methanol conversion alone does not demonstrate that CO2-based supply capability. CHEMREV-13, plastics returned to monomers below virgin-production cost and energy, shares the need to demonstrate an integrated economic and energy advantage, while addressing polymer recycling rather than methane conversion. No more specific technical overlap with CHEMREV-02, CHEMREV-03, CHEMREV-08, CHEMREV-09 or CHEMREV-10 can be established from their supplied titles.

Carbonate-fed electrochemical methane oxidation is the closest demonstrated adjacent approach in the supplied evidence. It shares the methane feedstock, methanol product and selective partial-oxidation objective, but uses electricity and carbonate rather than demonstrating the specified O2/air route. It informs the research problem and process evaluation without completing or redefining CHEMREV-12.

unresolved_issues: Whether a practically useful continuous O2- or air-fed route had been demonstrated by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
The Molecular Catalysis source's identity, characterization and mechanistic discussion require verification from source text.
The JACS report's ferrierite composition, oxidant, reaction conditions, rate and selectivity remain unverified in the supplied review.

The retained review does not establish the Kim study's single-pass methane conversion, sustained operating duration or full practical performance; these cannot be inferred from its reported rate and selectivity.
Useful quantitative thresholds for conversion, productivity, operating temperature, durability and plant economics remain application-dependent and have not been established here.

The review's recommendation to remove the unverified Molecular Catalysis and JACS details was not adopted literally: the user's requirement to preserve qualified quantitative and explanatory detail is met by retaining them as unverified attributions, separate from demonstrated results.
Related-concept comparisons rely on roster titles rather than full records, so detailed technical overlap remains unresolved.

brief.title: Making liquid methanol directly from methane
possible: Methane gas could become methanol, a transportable liquid chemical, in a continuous process using oxygen or air under mild conditions. A useful share of the methane would react, with most of the reacted carbon becoming methanol.
why: This could simplify methanol production by skipping synthesis gas, the intermediate used in the conventional route. Compact plants could also make methane at remote sites worth collecting and converting instead of burning it off.

sources.who: Authors of the Molecular Catalysis prospect
sources.showed: This prospect discusses the difficulty of converting methane selectively under mild conditions and preventing further oxidation of methanol.
sources.cited_for: It describes the chemical challenge of making methanol while protecting it from further reaction.
sources.not_established: A discussion of the chemical barriers does not demonstrate a continuous process using oxygen or air.

sources.showed: They used electricity to convert methane continuously at room temperature, with carbonate supplying oxygen. They reported that 93% of the reacted carbon became methanol.
sources.quote: enables efficient and selective electrochemical methane-to-methanol conversion at room temperature.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates continuous methane-to-methanol chemistry at room temperature using a different oxygen source.
sources.not_established: It does not establish useful methane conversion, lasting performance or a practical process fed with oxygen or air.

sources.who: Authors of the JACS methane-to-methanol report
sources.showed: This experimental report concerns methane conversion over ferrierite, a porous mineral catalyst, using nitrous oxide at elevated temperature.
sources.cited_for: It describes a related route using a different oxygen-supplying chemical.
sources.not_established: A heated process using nitrous oxide does not establish the intended mild process using oxygen or air.

shown: Kim and colleagues demonstrated continuous conversion at room temperature using electricity and carbonate, an oxygen-containing compound. Most of the reacted carbon became methanol. This establishes progress in related chemistry, but leaves the oxygen- or air-fed capability unresolved.
missing: A continuous oxygen- or air-fed process must combine useful methane conversion with methanol as the main carbon product under mild conditions.
Independent experiments must reproduce the performance and establish how long the catalyst keeps working.
An integrated process must recover methanol without excessive energy use, dilution or recycling of unreacted material.
A compact plant must demonstrate practical costs against a conventional alternative at the same scale.

milestones.label: Useful continuous conversion with methanol as the main product
milestones.explanation: Continuous operation with oxygen or air would have to turn a useful share of methane into mostly methanol under stated conditions. This would establish that recycling unreacted gas need not erase the benefit.

milestones.label: Complete process accounting and independently reproduced performance
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to account for inputs and products, measure recovered methanol quality, track sustained performance and reproduce the central result independently. This would establish reliability and expose hidden process burdens.

milestones.label: Competitive economics for a compact remote-gas plant
milestones.explanation: A complete assessment would have to compare a compact remote-gas plant with a conventional alternative at matching scale and product quality. This would test its practical value, with modeled gains remaining projections.

milestones.label: Production rate sufficient for the whole plant
milestones.explanation: The production rate would have to meet plant needs alongside conversion, product concentration, catalyst quantity, durability and energy use. This would establish whether laboratory output translates into useful production.

uncertain: The conversion, temperature, lifetime and cost targets that count as useful depend on the application.
How much methane reacts in a single pass through Kim’s process, and how long its performance lasts, remain unresolved.
Whether a continuous oxygen- or air-fed route already combines all the required capabilities remains unresolved.

page.title: Continuous aerobic methane-to-methanol conversion
page.definition: A continuous process converts methane directly to recovered methanol using molecular oxygen or air at room temperature, without synthesis gas (carbon monoxide plus hydrogen). It combines published hurdles for methane conversion, methanol selectivity and overall carbon utilization.

goal.need: Synthesis-gas generation accounts for around 60% of the capital cost of conventional methane-based methanol production. Direct conversion would bypass this intermediate, but its benefit depends on the complete process: an engineering evaluation found that carbon losses, oxygen supply, compression and cooling could erase the anticipated advantage.

figures.caption: Overall process efficiencies compared in a 2015 engineering evaluation
figures.note: These are not matched plant measurements. The conventional comparator has a larger capacity and includes product-purification losses. Thermal efficiency uses lower heating values.

completion.title: A continuous oxygen-fed process meets reaction and overall carbon-utilization hurdles at room temperature.
completion.criterion: An integrated, continuous methane/O₂- or air-fed process recovers methanol without synthesis gas at 25 ± 3 °C. It simultaneously achieves ≥5% single-pass methane conversion, approximately 75% or higher methanol carbon selectivity, and ≥75% overall carbon utilization. Conversion is the fraction of methane reacted; selectivity is the fraction of reacted carbon forming methanol. Overall carbon utilization is the fraction of fresh carbon input, including process fuel, recovered in methanol. The temperature interval adopts NETL's experimental room-temperature condition; it is not an external completion threshold.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of NETL's room-temperature objective and experimental conditions with published engineering performance hurdles.
completion.basis: DOE/NETL programme criteria, National Academies reports and engineering assessments were searched for a combined continuous O₂/air, temperature, conversion, selectivity and recovery test; none was found. This synthesis combines NETL's objective with Dummer et al.'s reaction and carbon-utilization hurdles. These are screening targets, not proof of cost competitiveness.

milestones.title: A laboratory catalyst makes methanol from methane and O₂ at room temperature.
milestones.criterion: A laboratory catalyst forms methanol from methane and O₂ at room temperature. Hao et al., published on 16 January 2025, report 4.37 mmol g−1 h−1 at 25 °C with 50 mg catalyst and 1:1 CH₄/O₂; Figure 4 uses three independent measurements. Their 210-hour continuous experiment instead operated near 75 °C, producing 14.4 mmol g−1 h−1 with approximately 100% selectivity and collected methanol at 0.25 mol L−1. Kim et al.'s 2025 continuous room-temperature result, approximately 11.1 mmol gcat−1 h−1, uses carbonate as oxygen source and does not establish the O₂-fed test.
milestones.set_by: DOE/NETL award DE-FE0031867, room-temperature objective, originally specified for photocatalysis; the oxygen-feed restriction follows this entry's scope.
milestones.threshold_quote: methanol can be formed at room temperature.

milestones.title: Methane conversion approaches 7–10% with 80–90% methanol selectivity in the same experiment.
milestones.criterion: Meet the project's published go/no-go criterion: approach 7–10% methane conversion with 80–90% methanol selectivity under commercially reasonable operating conditions. Neither 'approaching' nor those conditions is numerically defined. The 2024 presentation reports approximately 1% conversion and 90% liquid-product selectivity using 10 mg catalyst, 100 mL water, 6.89 bar CH₄, 2.76 bar O₂, 1 hour, 25 ± 3 °C and 365 nm illumination. The selectivity figure covers all liquid products. This programme presentation is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Stanford University/Susteon/Casale, DOE/NETL award DE-FE0031867, 2022 project schedule, go/no-go row; written for photocatalytic conversion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Test results show approaching 7-10% methane conversion with 80-90% methanol selectivity under commercially reasonable operating conditions.

milestones.title: A methane-to-methanol catalyst operates with simulated natural gas under intended process conditions.
milestones.criterion: The catalyst converts methane to methanol when supplied with simulated natural gas under conditions representative of its intended commercial application. Task 6 requires this operating performance test but specifies no numerical conversion, selectivity or lifetime minimum. The 2024 project schedule marks Task 6 complete; the opened presentation does not provide the simulated-gas composition and associated performance dataset.
milestones.set_by: Stanford University/Susteon/Casale, DOE/NETL award DE-FE0031867, Task 6; written for the project's photocatalytic catalyst.
milestones.threshold_quote: under realistic conditions with simulated natural gas for commercial application.

milestones.title: An engineering-scale methane-to-methanol prototype works under representative process conditions.
milestones.criterion: An integrated O₂/air-fed methane-to-methanol prototype demonstrates operation at engineering or pilot scale in an environment representative of its intended application. Its configuration includes the reactor and required feed handling, methanol recovery and recycle. This applies DOE's technology readiness level 6 test to the process; the guide specifies no universal production capacity or operating duration. A process simulation or pilot-plant design alone does not demonstrate this result.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, DOE G 413.3-4A, technology readiness level 6; a generic engineering criterion applied here, not a methanol-specific qualification.
milestones.threshold_quote: testing should be completed at an engineering or pilot scale, with a testing system fidelity that is similar to the actual application.
